territories.title: The Engine Works
territories.subtitle: Inference and Serving
territories.about:
Inference and serving is the work of running a trained model fast and cheaply. The central fact is that generating text is limited by memory, not arithmetic: a model writes one token at a time, and each step has to read all of its weights plus a KV cache holding attention state for every earlier token. The cache grows with context length and with every concurrent request, and much of this region is about fitting, sharing and shrinking it.

Serving engines solved the basic problems first. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave a batch at every step so the GPU never idles, PagedAttention stores the cache in small blocks like virtual memory so little is wasted, and FlashAttention computes attention without moving large matrices through slow memory. Quantization stores weights, and then the cache, in fewer bits, which also makes models small enough for laptops and phones. Speculative decoding has a fast drafter guess several tokens that the big model checks at once.

The current stack treats the KV cache as data to manage across a cluster. Prompt caching reuses it for shared prefixes, and providers bill cache hits as cheaper input tokens. Chunked prefill keeps long prompts from stalling other users, and disaggregated serving runs prompt processing and token generation on separate machines, shipping the cache between them and offloading it to CPU memory or SSD for reuse. From the application side the main levers are routing easy requests to cheaper models, ordering prompts so caches hit, and constrained decoding for guaranteed output formats. Landmarks worth knowing: the KV cache, continuous batching, PagedAttention, FlashAttention, quantization, speculative decoding and prompt caching. The open questions are mostly economic: how to trade time to first token, streaming speed and cost per token across very different workloads, long-running agents especially.

learningPath.title: Transformer Inference Arithmetic
learningPath.why: Works through the memory and compute math of generating one token at a time. It shows why decoding is limited by memory bandwidth and why the KV cache is the main thing to manage.

learningPath.title: Achieve 23x LLM Inference Throughput & Reduce p50 Latency
learningPath.why: Explains continuous batching and why paged KV memory makes it work. Read it to see how serving engines keep the GPU busy across many requests.

learningPath.title: A Visual Guide to Quantization
learningPath.why: Illustrated tour of number formats and the main weight quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF). It covers the most common way to fit a model into less memory.

learningPath.title: Looking back at speculative decoding
learningPath.by: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias (Google Research)
learningPath.why: The original authors explain how a cheap draft model plus one verification pass speeds up decoding without changing outputs. Start here before draft heads like EAGLE and Medusa.

learningPath.title: Fast and Expressive LLM Inference with RadixAttention and SGLang
learningPath.by: Lianmin Zheng, Ying Sheng et al. (LMSYS)
learningPath.why: Shows how reusing the KV cache across requests that share a prefix saves recomputation. This is the mechanism behind prefix and prompt caching.

learningPath.title: DistServe: disaggregating prefill and decoding for goodput-optimized LLM inference
learningPath.why: Explains why prefill and decode have different bottlenecks and why large deployments now run them on separate GPUs. It ties the earlier pieces into the shape of a modern serving stack.

territories.title: The Whispering Coast
territories.subtitle: Prompting and Context Engineering
territories.about:
Prompting and Context Engineering is about shaping what a model does purely through what you send it, without touching its weights. It began as prompt engineering: finding instructions and examples that got a pretrained model to do a task. As models went into products, prompts became software: templates, chains, system prompts, and schema-shaped outputs that code can parse.

Two branches grew from there. Programmatic optimization stops hand-tuning: methods like APE, DSPy and TextGrad generate and score prompt variants against a dataset and a metric, so prompts become compiled artifacts gated by evals. Context engineering arrived with agents: once a model runs for hundreds of turns with tools, the question shifts from how to word an instruction to what should be in the context window at all. Long windows didn't remove the problem, since models still miss material buried in the middle, so compaction, careful ordering, and progressive disclosure keep the working set small and relevant.

Landmarks worth knowing: few-shot prompting, structured outputs, declarative prompt compilation, and context engineering. The direction of travel is from writing prompts to engineering the whole input state, measured by evals.

learningPath.title: Prompt Engineering
learningPath.why: A compact map of the basic techniques (zero-/few-shot, example selection, chain-of-thought, automatic prompt design), with the papers behind each, before you go deeper on any one.

learningPath.title: Prompting 101 | Code w/ Claude
learningPath.why: Watch a production prompt get built and debugged step by step: system prompt, task context, examples, output format.

learningPath.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
learningPath.why: The experiment that showed where you put information in a long context changes whether the model uses it, which is why context engineering became its own discipline.

learningPath.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
learningPath.why: Shifts the question from wording one prompt to curating everything an agent sees over many turns: compaction, note-taking, sub-agents and just-in-time retrieval.

learningPath.title: Let the LLM Write the Prompts: An Intro to DSPy in Compound AI Pipelines
learningPath.why: A 30-minute practitioner case for treating prompts as optimizable parameters, showing a real pipeline improved with an optimizer instead of hand-tuning.

learningPath.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
learningPath.why: The formal version of that idea: signatures, modules and a compiler that bootstraps demonstrations and instructions against a metric.

territories.title: The Archival Reach
territories.subtitle: Retrieval and Knowledge
territories.about:
Retrieval and Knowledge covers how AI systems bring outside facts into the model's context, so answers rest on your documents rather than on what the model memorized. It grew out of classical search (BM25 keyword ranking) and neural embeddings, and took its modern shape in 2020 with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find relevant passages, put them in the prompt, generate.

The basic pipeline of chunk, embed and retrieve fails in predictable ways, and most of the region is fixes for them. Chunks lose their surrounding context, so contextual retrieval, late chunking and parent-document retrieval put it back. A single embedding vector blurs exact terms and fine detail, so production systems combine keyword and vector search, rerank candidates with a cross-encoder, and sometimes keep one vector per token (late interaction). Bad retrieval poisons the answer, so newer designs grade what they retrieved, retrieve again mid-answer, or hand search to an agent that issues its own queries, including grep and file reads over code.

Two debates shape the region today. Million-token context windows did not make retrieval obsolete: models get distracted by irrelevant material in long contexts, and sending everything costs far more per query, so systems increasingly choose between retrieval and long context per question. Graph-based retrieval answers global, multi-hop questions that passage search can't, but full GraphRAG indexing is expensive, and lighter variants defer most of the work to query time. Landmarks worth knowing: embeddings and dense retrieval, RAG, hybrid search with reranking, contextual retrieval, and agentic RAG.

learningPath.title: Stanford CS25: V3 I Retrieval Augmented Language Models
learningPath.why: One of the RAG paper's authors explains why a model's frozen weights go stale and make things up, and how pairing it with a retriever addresses both. A good map of the whole region before the details.

learningPath.title: Embeddings: What they are and why they matter
learningPath.why: A plain-language walk through what an embedding is and how similarity search over embeddings works, with runnable examples. This is the building block under dense retrieval.

learningPath.title: Beyond the Basics of Retrieval for Augmenting Generation (w/ Ben Clavié)
learningPath.by: Ben Clavié (Mastering LLMs conference, hosted by Hamel Husain)
learningPath.why: Lays out the production baseline step by step: keyword search alongside embeddings, a cross-encoder reranker on top, and where late-interaction models fit. Explains why a single vector search is rarely enough.

learningPath.title: Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems
learningPath.why: Measures how much each layer of the baseline helps (BM25 plus embeddings, then reranking) and adds one cheap fix: prefixing each chunk with a short note on where it came from before indexing.

learningPath.title: Long Context RAG Performance of LLMs
learningPath.why: Tests whether stuffing more retrieved text into long-context models keeps helping. Most models peak and then decline, which is the practical answer to 'do we still need retrieval?'

learningPath.title: The unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for agentic search — Jo Kristian Bergum, Hornet.dev
learningPath.why: When an agent writes its own search queries, they get longer and more specific, and plain keyword search becomes a strong tool again. A useful counterweight as retrieval moves inside agent loops.

territories.title: The Free Cities
territories.subtitle: Agents and Orchestration
territories.about:
Agents and Orchestration covers models that act: calling tools, running in loops, remembering across sessions, and working with other agents. It began with routing. MRKL sent parts of a request to calculators and APIs, Toolformer trained models to decide when to call tools themselves, and function calling made that a standard API: the model returns a structured call, your code runs it. ReAct wrapped this in the basic agent loop of think, act, observe, repeat.

Fully autonomous loops proved expensive and unpredictable in production, so most deployed systems moved back toward workflows: control flow written in code, with the model called only where judgment is needed. Autonomy survives where tasks are open-ended and the environment is safe to explore, above all in coding agents, which now run for hours across many context windows using progress files, memory, and subagents.

Protocols turned tools into shared infrastructure. MCP lets one server work with any client, Agent Skills package know-how an agent loads on demand, and code execution keeps bulky tool results out of the context window. Landmarks worth knowing: function calling, the ReAct loop, workflow graphs, MCP, and coding agents. The direction of travel is toward bounded, well-instrumented agents rather than unconstrained autonomy.

learningPath.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
learningPath.why: One map of the whole field (planning, memory, tool use) with the papers behind each part, so the later readings have somewhere to land.

learningPath.title: LLM Agents: History & Overview (UC Berkeley CS294-196)
learningPath.why: The ReAct author explains how agents grew out of reasoning plus acting, which is the loop every later system still runs.

learningPath.title: Building effective agents
learningPath.why: Separates workflows (control flow in code) from agents (the model chooses the steps) and names the common patterns, which is the main design choice you will face in practice.

learningPath.title: Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents
learningPath.why: Most agent failures trace back to tool design, and this covers naming, scoping, response size and how to evaluate tools.

learningPath.title: Building Agents with Model Context Protocol - Full Workshop
learningPath.why: Shows how tools become shared infrastructure through MCP, walking through servers, clients and how an agent uses them.

learningPath.title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
learningPath.why: Shows what changes when a task outlasts one context window: progress files, feature lists, one tested increment per session.

territories.title: The Peninsula of Long Thought
territories.subtitle: Planning and Reasoning
territories.about:
Planning and Reasoning covers how a model works its way to an answer instead of producing it in one shot. It starts with chain-of-thought: asking the model to write out intermediate steps before answering turned out to unlock multi-step math and logic in large models. Variations followed quickly. Self-consistency samples several chains and takes the majority answer, and program-aided reasoning has the model write code so an interpreter does the arithmetic.

A single chain can't recover from an early mistake, so the next step was search. Tree of Thoughts and its descendants treat partial reasoning as states to expand, score and backtrack from, and process reward models score each step so the search knows where to go. Planning researchers pushed further toward external checking: in LLM-Modulo systems the model only proposes plans and formal verifiers decide whether they are valid.

Since late 2024 much of this has moved inside the model. Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning to think at length before answering, and test-time compute became a dial: more thinking or more samples for a better answer at higher cost and latency. Landmarks worth knowing: chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree search, process reward models, and reasoning models. Open questions are whether the visible reasoning reflects what the model actually computed, which matters for anyone relying on it to monitor behavior, and whether reasoning will move out of text into hidden vectors.

learningPath.title: Stanford CS25: V5 I Large Language Model Reasoning, Denny Zhou of Google Deepmind
learningPath.why: One of the people behind chain-of-thought and self-consistency explains why intermediate steps help and how sampling, aggregation and RL fine-tuning build on that, which gives you the frame for everything in this region.

learningPath.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
learningPath.why: The paper that showed a few worked examples with written-out steps make large models much better at math and logic problems. Most later techniques here start from it.

learningPath.title: Why We Think
learningPath.why: A single long survey of test-time thinking: parallel sampling, sequential revision, search, reward models, latent thinking and faithfulness, with the papers behind each, so the node-level reading has somewhere to land.

learningPath.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
learningPath.why: Measures when spending more compute at answer time (search against a verifier, or revising answers) beats using a bigger model, and shows the best strategy depends on how hard the question is.

learningPath.title: Understanding Reasoning LLMs
learningPath.why: Explains how reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 are actually built (inference-time scaling, pure RL, SFT plus RL, distillation) in plain terms, which connects the prompting techniques above to today's trained thinkers.

learningPath.title: LLM-Modulo Frameworks as Compound AI Architectures for Robust Planning (& Reasoning)
learningPath.why: The skeptic's case: LLMs alone don't plan reliably, so pair them with external verifiers and solvers. Useful for deciding when to trust a model's plan and when to check it.

territories.title: The Tempering Grounds
territories.subtitle: Adaptation and Post-Training
territories.about:
Adaptation and Post-Training covers everything done to a model's weights after pretraining. Pretraining produces a model that continues text; post-training turns it into an assistant that follows instructions, matches a style, behaves safely, or reasons through hard problems. Prompting and retrieval change what a model sees, while this region changes the model itself.

The classic recipe, popularized by InstructGPT, has three stages: supervised fine-tuning on example answers, a reward model trained on human comparisons, and reinforcement learning (PPO) against that reward. It works but runs several models at once, and most later methods simplify it. DPO trains directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers with no reward model or RL loop, and spawned variants for unpaired thumbs-up data (KTO), single-stage training (ORPO), and fresh samples from the model being trained (online DPO). Constitutional AI replaced much of the human labeling with AI feedback. Reasoning models brought RL back: RL with verifiable rewards scores answers with checkers such as unit tests, and GRPO drops PPO's critic model to make that affordable. Distillation then passes the resulting skills on to small models.

For application teams, the practical tools are parameter-efficient. LoRA trains small add-on matrices instead of the full model, QLoRA does so over a 4-bit base on a single GPU, and DoRA and ReFT push efficiency further. Model merging combines fine-tunes by weight arithmetic with no training at all. Landmarks worth knowing: SFT, LoRA, RLHF, DPO, RLVR with GRPO, and distillation.

learningPath.title: Training Overview (RLHF Book)
learningPath.why: A map of the modern post-training pipeline: instruction tuning, preference tuning and RL, and how labs chain them. Read it first so every later technique has a place to sit.

learningPath.title: Stanford CS336 Language Modeling from Scratch | Spring 2025 | Lecture 15: Alignment - SFT/RLHF
learningPath.why: A university lecture that walks from supervised fine-tuning to the classic RLHF setup, with the data and objectives spelled out. It gives the foundation the rest of the path builds on.

learningPath.title: LoRA Without Regret - Thinking Machines Lab
learningPath.why: Careful experiments on when low-rank fine-tuning matches full fine-tuning and which settings matter. It is the practical side of adapting a model on a budget.

learningPath.title: LLM Training: RLHF and Its Alternatives
learningPath.why: Explains the reward-model-plus-PPO recipe and the simpler preference methods (DPO and others) that grew up around it. Read it to see why the preference-optimization family exists.

learningPath.title: The State of Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
learningPath.why: Covers RL with verifiable rewards, GRPO and the reasoning-model papers that followed DeepSeek-R1. It brings the region up to the current frontier.

learningPath.title: The Rise of Reasoning Models | Post-Training Course Lecture 5
learningPath.why: A lecture from someone who builds open post-training recipes, on how RL for reasoning is done in practice. A good closing view of where post-training is heading.

territories.title: The Quarries
territories.subtitle: Data and Synthetic Data
territories.about: Creating, curating, and cleaning the data an AI system is built, tuned and tested on — golden and eval sets, model-assisted labeling, data flywheels from production traffic, synthetic generation, and corpus hygiene (deduplication, decontamination, quality filtering).

territories.title: The Watchtowers
territories.subtitle: Evaluation and Observability
territories.about:
Evaluation and Observability is how teams find out whether an AI system works, and why it doesn't. Old NLP metrics like BLEU and ROUGE counted word overlap with a reference answer, which says nothing about whether an open-ended answer is right, so the field rebuilt measurement around benchmarks, human preference votes, and, above all, models grading other models.

LLM-as-a-judge is the region's center. A strong model with a rubric agrees with human raters about as often as humans agree with each other, which made evaluation cheap enough to run on every change. Most of what surrounds it is about making judges trustworthy: swapping answer order to cancel position bias, reading score probabilities instead of a single number, training small dedicated judge models, and using a few human labels to correct a judge's aggregate score. Specialized evals grew out of this for RAG (was the right context found, and is the answer grounded in it?), for long context (can the model find a needle in a haystack?), and for agents, where benchmarks like SWE-bench check whether a task got done and trajectory evals grade the steps along the way.

The engineering side borrows from software practice. Eval-driven development runs eval suites in CI the way tests gate code, layering cheap deterministic checks under model-graded ones. Tracing records each model call, retrieval and tool call as spans, now with shared OpenTelemetry conventions, and online evaluation scores sampled production traffic to catch drift. Landmarks worth knowing: capability and agent benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge, RAG evaluation, eval-driven development, and tracing.

learningPath.title: Your AI Product Needs Evals
learningPath.why: The clearest case for why evals sit at the centre of building with LLMs, and how unit tests, human review and model graders fit together.

learningPath.title: Let's talk about LLM evaluation
learningPath.why: A tour of the three ways models get scored (automatic benchmarks, human judges, model judges) from someone who ran the Open LLM Leaderboard. It shows what public benchmarks can and cannot tell you.

learningPath.title: Using LLM-as-a-Judge For Evaluation: A Complete Guide
learningPath.why: How to build a model grader that agrees with a domain expert, step by step. This is the workhorse technique of the whole region.

learningPath.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLM-Evaluators (aka LLM-as-Judge)
learningPath.why: A survey of the research on model judges: their biases, when they agree with people, and the fine-tuned alternatives. Read it once you have built a judge and want to know where it can fail.

learningPath.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
learningPath.why: Carries the ideas over to agents, where a task has many steps and you grade both the outcome and the path taken.

learningPath.title: Evaluate Production Traffic - Langfuse
learningPath.why: Closes the loop: run the same graders on sampled live traces, so evaluation continues after you ship.

territories.title: The Bulwark
territories.subtitle: Safety, Security and Governance
territories.about:
Safety, Security and Governance covers keeping AI systems from causing harm, whether through attacks, mistakes or misuse. Early on that meant filtering offensive output. Once models could read outside content and take actions, it became a security field: prompt injection showed that any text a model reads can act as an instruction, and agents with tools turned that into a way to leak data or take actions for an attacker.

Defenses come in layers because none is complete. Guardrails screen what goes in and out. Injection defenses help the model tell instructions from data, by training it to rank sources by privilege (the instruction hierarchy), by marking untrusted text (spotlighting), or by designing the system so the model that reads untrusted text cannot act (the dual LLM pattern). Sandboxing and scoped permissions limit how much damage a hijacked agent can do. Red teaming, increasingly automated with attacker models, looks for the gaps before release.

Interpretability is starting to become a control tool as well as a research field. Sparse autoencoders and representation engineering find concepts inside a model's activations, and circuit breakers and unlearning act on them directly. Governance rests on documentation (model and system cards) and on provenance tools such as watermarking. Landmarks worth knowing: prompt injection and its indirect form, guardrails, agent sandboxing, red teaming, and model cards.

learningPath.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
learningPath.why: A checklist of the ten risks that come up most in real LLM applications, from prompt injection to excessive agency. It gives you the vocabulary and the overall picture before any one topic.

learningPath.title: Prompt Injection, explained
learningPath.why: The person who named prompt injection explains why mixing trusted instructions with untrusted text is the root problem, and why filters and clever prompting do not fix it.

learningPath.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
learningPath.why: A readable summary of six system designs (plan-then-execute, dual LLM, code-then-execute and others) that limit what injected text can do. The defences come from how the system is built rather than from the model.

learningPath.title: Making Claude Code more secure and autonomous with sandboxing
learningPath.why: A worked example of limiting an agent's damage through filesystem and network isolation. It also shows how a sandbox cuts the number of permission prompts a user has to answer.

learningPath.title: Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products
learningPath.by: Blake Bullwinkel et al. (Microsoft AI Red Team)
learningPath.why: Eight practical lessons from testing real products: start from what the system can actually do, simple attacks often beat gradient-based ones, and automation helps but humans still matter.

learningPath.title: Interpretability: Understanding how AI models think
learningPath.by: Anthropic (Josh Batson, Emmanuel Ameisen, Jack Lindsey)
learningPath.why: Three researchers explain in plain terms how they look inside a model to see what it is computing, and why that could become a way to check and steer behaviour rather than only test outputs.

territories.title: The Agora
territories.subtitle: AI Product and Interaction Design
territories.about:
AI Product and Interaction Design is about how AI reaches people: the screens, conversations and controls that sit between a model and its user. It grew out of HCI work on mixed-initiative systems, and Microsoft's 2019 guidelines for human-AI interaction still frame the basics: set expectations, explain behavior, make correction cheap.

The modern era began with two surfaces. Copilots (2021) put suggestions inline where users already work, and chat (2022) made a message thread the default way to talk to a model. Streaming made replies feel fast, and citations let users check grounded answers. Chat's linear thread is a poor place to build something, so canvases and artifacts moved the work product into an editable pane beside the conversation, and generative UI lets the model answer with interface components instead of prose.

Agents shifted the focus from what the model says to what it does. Approval gates pause before consequential actions, plan previews let users fix a plan before work starts, and action traces show what actually happened. Recent studies find that reviewing only an agent's final result misses errors made early in the run, which is pushing products toward step-level visibility and steering. Reasoning models added a visible thinking panel, which helps users follow along but is not a faithful explanation of how the answer was reached.

Landmarks worth knowing: the human-AI interaction guidelines, chat, copilots, citations, and human-in-the-loop approval. The open problem is trust calibration: getting users to rely on AI when it is right and check it when it is not, as outputs become longer, more autonomous and harder to verify.

learningPath.title: Guidelines for human-AI interaction design
learningPath.why: The 18 tested guidelines (set expectations, support correction, explain behavior, adapt over time) give a checklist that still applies to every pattern later in this region.

learningPath.title: Why Chatbots Are Not the Future of Interfaces
learningPath.why: Explains what a bare text box hides from users (what the tool can do, how to ask) and why most AI features need more structure than chat.

learningPath.title: Generative Interfaces Beyond Chat
learningPath.why: Shows concrete alternatives to chat, with the model's output turned into things the user can see, point at and edit directly.

learningPath.title: Agentic UX Patterns: A Practical Guide to Designing AI That Acts
learningPath.why: Covers the shift from answering to acting: plan previews, approvals, live action traces, and pause, stop and take-over controls, each with when to use it.

learningPath.title: AI Agent UX Patterns: Lessons From 1000 Startups
learningPath.why: A survey of how shipped agent products actually present their work to users, and which of those patterns hold up.

learningPath.title: Overreliance on AI: Literature Review
learningPath.why: Explains why people accept wrong AI output and which interface choices (explanations, uncertainty, friction) help them check it instead.

territories.title: The Painted Isles
territories.subtitle: Multimodal
territories.about:
Multimodal covers AI that works with images, audio, video and documents, not just text. It started with alignment: CLIP (2021) trained image and text encoders so a picture and its caption land close together, giving models a shared vocabulary for both. Vision-language models then fed those image vectors into a language model as extra tokens, and training on visual instructions turned them into assistants that read screenshots, charts and photos. Later models take images at their native resolution, which made small text and dense layouts readable, and sample frames to follow video.

Documents were one of the first places this paid off. Pipelines that chain layout detection and OCR lose reading order and garble tables, so vision models that read a whole page and output structured text are replacing them, and visual retrieval such as ColPali searches page images directly. Speech went the same way. Whisper made transcription a commodity, audio language models turned sound into tokens a language model can predict, and realtime voice moved from slow recognize-think-speak chains to single models that hear and speak audio, some of them listening and talking at once.

Generation runs on a separate line. Diffusion models create images by removing noise step by step; latent diffusion made text-to-image practical, transformers replaced the U-Net inside, and flow matching cut the number of steps. The same machinery, applied to patches across space and time, produces video. Landmarks worth knowing: CLIP, vision-language models, document understanding, Whisper, realtime voice, and latent diffusion. The open problems are mostly practical: images and audio use many tokens, so cost and latency dominate design, and generated video and speech still need better control.

learningPath.title: Multimodality and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)
learningPath.why: Explains why models need more than text, then walks through CLIP and Flamingo, the two designs most later vision-language systems build on.

learningPath.title: Vision Language Models (Better, faster, stronger)
learningPath.by: Hugging Face (Merve Noyan, Sergio Paniego et al.)
learningPath.why: A current survey of how vision-language models are built and used: model families, video input, smaller models, and the uses engineers actually ship.

learningPath.title: ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models
learningPath.why: Shows the problem with text-extraction pipelines for PDFs and how searching page images directly avoids it, which is the core idea of the documents part of this region.

learningPath.title: Voice AI & Voice Agents: An Illustrated Primer
learningPath.why: A practical guide to building voice agents: the latency budget, transcription, turn detection, interruptions, and when to use speech-to-speech models instead of a pipeline.

learningPath.title: The Illustrated Stable Diffusion

learningPath.title: Building Generative Image & Video models at Scale
learningPath.why: Covers how today's image and video generators are built, from latent spaces and denoising to conditioning and post-training, from someone who works on Veo.

landmarks.maturityNote: Delimiting untrusted text is common practice; datamarking and encoding are less widely adopted.
landmarks.desc: Transforming untrusted text before it reaches the model (delimiting it, interleaving a marker, or encoding it) so the model can see which text is data and not follow it.

The simplest version wraps it in delimiters; stronger ones put a special marker between every word (datamarking) or encode the whole text, and the system prompt says never to follow instructions inside marked text. landmarks.name: Dual LLM Pattern
landmarks.maturityNote: A widely cited design; production systems mostly use partial versions of it.
landmarks.desc: Splitting an assistant into a privileged model that calls tools but never sees untrusted text, and a quarantined model that reads untrusted text but cannot act, with ordinary code passing references between them.

A privileged model takes the user's instructions and calls tools but never sees untrusted text; a quarantined model reads that text (a web page, an email) but has no tools. Plain code between them hands the quarantined model's output to tools as opaque variables, so injected instructions have nothing to trigger. landmarks.name: Human-in-the-Loop Approval
landmarks.maturityNote: Essential for agents taking real actions.
landmarks.desc: Agents pause before consequential actions and ask the user to approve, edit, or reject them.

landmarks.name: Reasoning Trace Display
landmarks.maturityNote: Every major assistant shows some form of it; raw versus summarized traces and how much to show are still unsettled.

landmarks.name: Plan Preview
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard in coding and research agents; how detailed plans should be is still unsettled.

landmarks.name: Mid-Run Steering
landmarks.maturityNote: Evidence comes from recent studies; most products offer only interrupt-and-redirect.
landmarks.desc: Users inspect and redirect an agent step by step while it runs, rather than reviewing only the final result.
landmarks.summary: Instead of reviewing a long agent run only at the end, the user follows it step by step and corrects course while it works. A Microsoft Research study of spreadsheet agents found that end-of-run review misses errors buried in early steps, while step-level participation caught them and left users understanding the result. landmarks.name: Trust Calibration
landmarks.maturityNote: Well studied in HCI, but production products rarely go beyond disclaimers and citations.
landmarks.desc: Designing interfaces so users rely on AI output when it is right and check it when it is not, through uncertainty display, framing and friction.
landmarks.summary: The goal is appropriate reliance: users accept the AI's output when it is right and catch it when it is wrong. Too much trust (automation bias) lets errors through, and too little wastes the tool. Levers include showing uncertainty, framing what the system is good at, and adding friction where mistakes are costly. Research shows simple, intuitive uncertainty cues help, while complex statistical displays tend to be ignored.

landmarks.name: Turn-Taking and Barge-In
landmarks.maturityNote: Expected in voice agents since 2024; semantic turn detection is newer and still tuned per product.

Older assistants waited for a fixed silence, which cut people off mid-thought or left awkward gaps. landmarks.desc: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process, now standard for images, audio, and video.
landmarks.summary: A model is trained to remove a little noise from a noisy image. To generate, it starts from pure noise and denoises step by step until a clean image appears. The approach is stable to train and produces high-quality images, audio and video, at the cost of many sampling steps.

landmarks.name: Dynamic Resolution Encoding
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard in current VLMs; exposed to engineers as resolution and image-token settings.
landmarks.desc: Feeding images to a vision-language model at their native size and aspect ratio, so the number of visual tokens grows with the image instead of being squeezed into a fixed grid.
landmarks.summary: Early vision-language models shrank every image to a small fixed square, which made small text, dense charts and screen details unreadable. Newer models cut the image into tiles or patches at its own resolution and use 2D position encodings, so a large image becomes more tokens. Detail improves, but an image's token cost now depends on its size, which engineers control with resolution settings.

landmarks.name: Audio Language Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Behind current speech synthesis and voice models; voice cloning raises open consent and misuse questions.
landmarks.desc: Language models trained on discrete audio tokens from a neural codec, predicting audio the way text models predict words; the basis of modern speech synthesis and end-to-end voice models.
landmarks.summary: A neural audio codec compresses sound into a sequence of discrete tokens, and a language model learns to predict the next one, exactly as a text model predicts the next word. This produces natural speech and music, and from a few seconds of a speaker's voice it can continue in that voice (zero-shot text-to-speech). The same audio tokens let end-to-end voice assistants hear and speak without converting to text.

landmarks.name: Full-Duplex Voice Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Open research models and early products; most deployed voice agents still use turn detection.
landmarks.desc: Speech models that model the user's and the agent's audio as two parallel streams, so they listen and speak at the same time with no explicit turn boundaries.
landmarks.summary: Most voice assistants take turns: they wait for you to stop, then answer. A full-duplex model processes your audio and its own as two streams at once, frame by frame, so overlaps, interruptions and small acknowledgements like "uh-huh" are handled by the model itself. Moshi also predicts a text version of its own speech slightly ahead of the audio, which keeps answers coherent, and responds in about 200 ms.

landmarks.name: Flow Matching
landmarks.maturityNote: The default objective for many 2024+ generators; diffusion remains common.
landmarks.desc: Training a generator to follow a learned velocity field from noise to data, usually along straight paths, instead of learning to reverse a noising process.
landmarks.summary: An alternative training objective to diffusion. Instead of learning to remove noise step by step, the model learns which direction to move at each point to get from noise to an image, with the paths kept close to straight lines. Straighter paths need fewer sampling steps, and training is simpler. Recent image, video and speech models such as Stable Diffusion 3 and Flux use it.
